summary: Pinaverium bromide is a gut-selective calcium channel blocker used as an antispasmodic for the symptomatic treatment of pain, bowel disturbance and discomfort in irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) and related functional gastrointestinal disorders, and for pain related to functional biliary disorders. It acts locally on intestinal smooth muscle with minimal systemic cardiovascular effect. It is not FDA-approved in the US (used in Europe, Latin America, Canada and Asia); this record is based on SmPC/EMA-style regional labeling. The usual adult dose is 50 mg three times daily, increasing to a maximum of 100 mg twice daily, taken with water during meals; because it can cause esophageal irritation it must not be taken lying down or just before bed.

moa: Pinaverium bromide is a selective L-type calcium channel antagonist acting on gastrointestinal smooth muscle. By blocking calcium influx into intestinal and biliary smooth-muscle cells it reduces muscle hyperreactivity and spasm, relieving spasmodic pain and modulating motility. Its quaternary ammonium structure limits systemic absorption and confers gut selectivity, so it has little effect on cardiovascular calcium channels.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to pinaverium bromide or any excipient
relative: Conditions predisposing to esophageal retention or stricture
Inability to take the tablet upright with adequate fluid
monitor: Symptom response and need for continued therapy

preg: There are insufficient data on use in pregnancy; it is generally not recommended and should be used only if clearly necessary after assessing benefit versus risk. Follow current SmPC guidance.
lact: It is not known whether pinaverium passes into breast milk in clinically relevant amounts; in the absence of adequate data, use during breastfeeding is generally not recommended.
renal: No specific dose adjustment is required for renal impairment because systemic absorption and renal elimination are limited; use the usual cautions.
hepatic: Pinaverium undergoes hepatic metabolism; use with caution in hepatic impairment and reserve for clear need, following SmPC guidance.

major: No clinically significant major interactions are well established at recommended doses
moderate: Other agents that can cause esophageal irritation may add to local mucosal risk
minor: Theoretical additive effect with other antispasmodics on gut motility
interactions.food: Should be taken with food (during meals) to improve tolerability and reduce esophageal contact; no specific food must be avoided.
interactions.alcohol: No specific interaction is established; moderation is advisable as alcohol can aggravate GI symptoms.
interactions.diagnostics: No characteristic laboratory interference; relaxes GI smooth muscle, which is exploited when used as preparation for radiologic/endoscopic examination.

serious: Esophageal irritation or ulceration if taken incorrectly (without water or while lying down)

Severe odynophagia or chest pain suggesting esophageal injury

pearls: Not FDA-approved in the US but used in Europe, Latin America, Canada and Asia; this record uses SmPC/EMA-style references
Gut-selective L-type calcium channel blocker - acts on intestinal/biliary smooth muscle with minimal cardiovascular effect
Always take with water during meals and never lying down - poor administration can cause esophageal irritation/ulceration
Used for IBS and functional GI/biliary pain; treats symptoms, not the underlying cause
Low systemic absorption means few systemic drug interactions and no renal dose adjustment
missed: If a dose is missed, take it as soon as remembered with water during food; if it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and continue the regular schedule. Do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one.
overdose: Experience with overdose is limited. Management is supportive and symptomatic; there is no specific antidote. Treat as for ingestion of a quaternary-ammonium antispasmodic with monitoring and supportive care, and contact a poison control center.
